newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian leader rejects calls for him to quit.
newsitem.headline: Albanian leader rejects calls for him to quit.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha was quoted on Sunday as rejecting calls to resign from rebels holding the south of the country and urging the international community to help avert civil war.
His appeal, in an interview with the Rome newspaper La Repubblica, came as Italy flew emergency medical aid to the rebel stronghold of Vlore in the south.

It also came on the eve of a meeting of European Union foreign ministers to discuss how to provide security for a major humanitarian relief mission to the Balkan country, battered by weeks of turmoil.

The EU has already turned down an Albanian request for large-scale military intervention to help restore order after rebels looted weapons from army depots and rose against Berisha, blaming him for failed savings schemes that bankrupted thousands, and the anarchy spread throughout the country.
Berisha dismissed the rebels' demands for his resignation, saying: "I will not submit to blackmail, I will not let myself be frightened by the threat of arms."
"My future is in the hands of the Albanian people. I won't leave politics but I will respect, without any hesitation, any decision of the people. This too is democracy."
Berisha has promised to quit if his party loses new elections to be held by June.
Berisha said he wanted the international community to help Albania "avert civil war and help us put the country back on its feet".
Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino has also rebuffed the rebels in the south, saying Berisha's resignation now would create a power vacuum, but offered to open a dialogue with them.
Fino is due to travel to Rome on Tuesday to discuss the Albanian crisis with EU foreign ministers at a meeting to mark the 40th anniversary of the founding of the European Economic Community.

Fino, a member of the opposition Socialist Party, has been locked in a power struggle with Berisha's Democrats, who control 122 of the 140 seats in parliament after elections last May that international observers said were deeply flawed.
In Vlore, Italian helicopters brought in nearly two tonnes of medical aid in an operation organised by rebel councils now running southern towns and the Italian government.
"We are happy such an operation was successful because we badly needed medical equipment," local hospital director Servet Kojdheli told Reuters.
Kojdheli said up to six Italian surgeons were due to be flown into Vlore on Monday to operate on over 50 people seriously wounded and dozens more slightly injured during the turmoil.
The Italian government is also due to fly medical aid to the capital Tirana in the north of the country, which is under government control, following a request from Fino.

The Interior Ministry announced on Sunday that the northern port of Durres, some 40 km (25 miles) west of Tirana, had reopened. It was closed last week after scenes of chaos as thousands of Albanians tried to flee in rusty ships.
In Tirana several hundred people, many of them mothers with their children, staged a demonstration to demand an end to the violent unrest that has gripped the country.
They held up placards saying "Stop violence and weapons" and "Give the children books, not guns".
